title: Narada sings the names
hook: a harmonium, a drum, one voice, and a whole room singing it back
tomorrow: who are the singers with a drum on the city sidewalk?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Narada asked Brahma for the chant's rules and heard there were none: the names of God need no rules. Today, the last part: the names sung together.
screen: `NO RULES OF TIME, PLACE OR PURITY.`

segments.voice: A student hall on a Friday night, chairs pushed to the walls. Someone pumps a harmonium and it wheezes into a chord. A drum picks up the beat. One voice sings a short line of names, and the room sings it back, a little ragged. Then again, a little faster. At the back, a first-timer who swears she can't sing is reading the words off a friend's lips. A few rounds in, her mouth is moving. Soon, nobody in the room is the audience. How did that happen?
screen: `A HARMONIUM WHEEZES INTO A CHORD.` → `ONE VOICE, THEN THE ROOM.` → `NOBODY IS THE AUDIENCE.`

segments.voice: That's kirtan: singing God's names and glories, often in call and response. And the Bhagavata Purana has a singer at its heart. Narada tells the sage Vyasa his own story. In an earlier life he was a servant woman's little boy, sweeping and fetching for wandering sages who stayed through one rainy season. Every day he heard them sing about the Lord, and the singing got into him. When his mother died, the boy walked off alone, sat under a tree and, for one moment, saw God in his heart. Then the vision was gone, and a voice told him the longing it left would carry him home. Now Narada wanders the worlds with his vina, and he says that when he sings the Lord's names, the Lord appears in his heart, as if called. A servant boy who could perform no grand ritual, made a sage by hearing and singing. That's why the same Purana says that in the age of Kali the wise worship through sankirtana, singing the names together. Not a sacrifice only priests can perform. A song the one at the back can join. A pop chorus with a chant in it is not a kirtan. But it carried the sound of one home, and soon someone would take the singing out onto the street.
screen: `NARADA: A SERVANT BOY WHO HEARD THE SAGES SING.` · `HE SINGS, AND THE LORD APPEARS IN HIS HEART.` · `SANKIRTANA: THE WORSHIP OF THE WISE.` · `A SONG THE ONE AT THE BACK CAN JOIN.` · then, large: `THE ROOM ANSWERS THE VOICE.`

segments.voice: Try a little kirtan on your own. Pick a short line of names Hindus sing, like Hare Krishna, Hare Rama, or Om Namah Shivaya; if you don't pray, one word you hold dear. Sing or hum it softly, then pause, as if a room were singing it back, and let the pause be as full as the line. Keep that rhythm, call and quiet answer, until the breath settles into it.
The Beatles and the mantra: from a silent word in Rishikesh to names sung together in kirtan, the last stop on this road.
screen: `THE BEATLES AND THE MANTRA — today's word`.

segments.voice: For the road, from Narada's song: sankirtana, God's names sung together, where the room answers the voice. Until tomorrow.

fork.setup: at a family puja, your uncle leads a bhajan and your teenage cousins stand at the back with their phones, 'just watching.' what would make it kirtan?
options: everyone answering the line, even softly, so no one is just watching.
a better speaker, so the leader's voice reaches the back of the room.
a trained singer up front, so the music sounds the way it should.
fork.reveal: kirtan is call and response: one voice sings the names, and the room sings them back. the Bhagavata calls singing them together the worship of the wise.
